stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Reyes's conclusion?
stimulus: Steel expansion joints let a bridge deck lengthen on hot days and shorten on cold ones. On the Harlow Viaduct, several of these joints have rusted and jammed, and inspectors have found cracked concrete beside each jammed joint. After reviewing the inspection reports, engineer Tomas Reyes concluded that the cracking was caused by the jammed joints, which prevented the deck from expanding as temperatures rose.
choices: Cracking just as severe appears beside the viaduct's joints that still move freely.
Cracks beside the jammed joints widened most during the hottest weeks of summer.
The viaduct's expansion joints were installed when the bridge opened forty years ago.
Inspectors found no cracked concrete beside any of the viaduct's jammed joints.
explanation: Reyes's conclusion holds only if the jammed joints make the difference. If concrete beside joints that move freely cracks just as badly, then jamming can't explain the damage, because something else is causing it. That removes the condition his conclusion depends on.

B.why: You answered the opposite question. Cracks widening in the hottest weather fit Reyes's idea that the deck can't expand, so this finding supports his conclusion instead of weakening it.

C.why: You picked a detail on the right topic that doesn't test the claim. The age of the joints says nothing about whether jamming causes the cracks.

D.why: The passage says inspectors found cracked concrete beside each jammed joint. A finding has to be possible within the scenario, and this one reverses a fact the passage states.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Osei's hypothesis?
stimulus: Some nutritionists argue that eating breakfast helps students concentrate during morning classes. To test this idea, researcher Amara Osei recruited two groups of high school students who were similar in age, sleep habits, and class schedules. One group ate a breakfast of oatmeal and fruit before school, and the other ate nothing. Osei hypothesizes that the breakfast group will score higher than the other group on an attention test given at mid-morning.
choices: The two groups earned nearly identical scores on the mid-morning attention test.
The breakfast group scored well above the other group on the mid-morning test.
Most students in both groups said they preferred oatmeal to other breakfast foods.
Osei's study included a single group of students, all of whom ate breakfast.
explanation: Settle the direction first: if Osei is right, the breakfast group should score higher. If the two groups' scores were nearly identical, breakfast made no difference to attention, and that is exactly the result her hypothesis predicts won't happen.

B.why: This is the result Osei predicts, so it strengthens her hypothesis. You missed the word 'weaken' in the question.

C.why: Students' food preferences are about breakfast but say nothing about how well they concentrate. Matching the topic doesn't make a finding bear on the hypothesis.

D.why: The passage describes two groups, one of which ate nothing. This choice changes how the study was set up instead of reporting a result from it.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Haruto's claim?
stimulus: Telescope observations have revealed a thin ring of dust circling Kessa-9, a small icy body far beyond Neptune. Kessa-9 also has a tiny moon, which orbits inside the ring. Small meteoroids strike this moon from time to time, blasting fine material off its surface. Planetary scientist Lin Haruto claims that the ring is supplied with dust mainly by these impacts on the moon.
choices: The ring's dust has a chemical makeup unlike that of the moon's surface material.
The ring's dust has a chemical makeup that matches the moon's surface material.
Kessa-9 takes roughly three hundred years to complete one orbit around the Sun.
Most rings in the solar system are made of large ice chunks rather than dust.
explanation: If the ring's dust really comes from the moon, it should be made of the same material as the moon's surface. Dust with a different chemical makeup must come from somewhere else, so this finding undercuts Haruto's claim.

B.why: A chemical match is what Haruto's claim predicts, so this supports the claim. You chose the finding that sounded most connected to the passage instead of the one that cuts against it.

C.why: How long Kessa-9 takes to orbit the Sun has nothing to do with where its ring dust comes from. It's a fact about the right object that doesn't touch the claim.

D.why: A general pattern about other rings can't tell you about this ring, which the passage says is made of dust. You stretched a broad claim to a case it doesn't cover.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Delgado's claim?
stimulus: Painted bike lanes are a common way for cities to encourage cycling. In 2021, Marlow City added such lanes to twenty streets, some of them busy commercial streets and others quiet residential ones. After comparing cycling counts from before and after the change, urban planner Rosa Delgado claims that the new lanes increased cycling on Marlow's busy commercial streets in particular.
choices: Cycling counts on Marlow's commercial streets were no higher after 2021 than before.
Cycling counts on Marlow's commercial streets roughly doubled in the year after 2021.
Cycling counts on Marlow's quiet residential streets stayed about the same after 2021.
Marlow City did not add bike lanes to any of its streets during 2021 or afterward.
explanation: Delgado's claim is limited to busy commercial streets, and it requires cycling there to have gone up after the lanes were added. If counts on those streets didn't rise, the increase she describes didn't happen.

B.why: A doubling in cycling on commercial streets is exactly what Delgado claims, so this strengthens her claim. You answered the opposite of what the question asks.

C.why: Delgado makes no claim about residential streets. 'In particular' limits her claim to commercial streets, so a result for a group outside that scope can't weaken it.

D.why: The passage says Marlow added lanes to twenty streets in 2021. This choice denies a fact the passage states instead of offering a finding about cycling.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Marsh's argument?
stimulus: Several printed maps of the Calder coast from the 1700s show a long sandbar near the harbor mouth, but charts made after 1850 leave it out. Historian Ines Marsh notes that eighteenth-century mapmakers often copied coastlines from older maps instead of surveying the coast themselves. She argues that the sandbar never existed and was simply copied from one inaccurate original map.
choices: Ship logs from the 1700s record vessels running aground on a sandbar at that spot.
Every map showing the sandbar can be traced back to a single map drawn in 1702.
Maps of the Calder coast from the 1700s were printed in several different languages.
Charts of the Calder coast made after 1850 also show the long sandbar near the harbor.
explanation: Marsh's argument depends on the sandbar being imaginary. Ship logs recording groundings at that spot are independent, firsthand evidence that a real sandbar was there, which offers a better explanation for why the maps show it than copying does.

B.why: Tracing every map back to one original is what Marsh's copying explanation predicts, so this supports her argument. You backed the claim the question asks you to challenge.

C.why: What languages the maps were printed in tells you nothing about whether the sandbar was real or copied. The finding is about the maps but not about the argument.

D.why: The passage says charts made after 1850 leave the sandbar out. This choice reverses that fact instead of adding new evidence.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Okafor's hypothesis?
stimulus: After a hard workout, some athletes sit in cold water for ten minutes. They do it to ease the muscle soreness that peaks about a day later. Sports scientist Leah Okafor had 40 cyclists complete identical training sessions. Half then sat in cold water and half rested at room temperature. Okafor hypothesizes that cold-water immersion reduces next-day muscle soreness.
choices: Cyclists who sat in cold water reported less soreness the next day than cyclists who rested.
Cyclists in both groups reported about the same level of soreness on the day after training.
Cyclists who sat in cold water said the first few minutes of immersion felt unpleasant.
Cold water eased next-day soreness in the cyclists and also in a separate group of runners.
explanation: The question asks you to weaken the hypothesis that cold water reduces next-day soreness. For that to be true, the cold-water group has to end up less sore than the group that rested. If both groups report about the same soreness, the cold water made no difference, and that removes the hypothesis's only support.

A.why: You answered the opposite question. Less soreness in the cold-water group is exactly what Okafor predicts, so this choice strengthens her hypothesis.

C.why: You picked a detail about the cyclists' experience. The hypothesis is about soreness the next day, not about how the water felt, so this neither supports nor weakens it.

D.why: This choice supports the hypothesis and then extends it to runners the study never tested. You were asked to weaken the claim, not to make it broader.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Reyes's conclusion?
stimulus: Wetlands act like sponges: they soak up rainwater and release it slowly. In 2019, farmland along the upper Marren River was restored to wetland so that less water would reach the river all at once. Hydrologist Tomas Reyes concluded that the restoration lowered peak flows at a downstream gauge during heavy spring storms.
choices: During heavy spring storms after the restoration, downstream peak flows were lower than before it.
During heavy spring storms after the restoration, downstream peak flows were no lower than before it.
During light summer rains after the restoration, downstream peak flows were no lower than before it.
Since the restoration, the wetlands have attracted more nesting birds than the farmland once did.
explanation: Reyes's conclusion is narrow: peak flows at the downstream gauge fell during heavy spring storms. For it to hold, flows in those storms have to drop after 2019. If heavy-storm peaks were no lower than before, the claimed effect never happened.

A.why: You answered the opposite question. Lower peak flows in heavy storms is exactly what Reyes concluded, so this choice supports him.

C.why: You missed the scope words. Reyes's conclusion covers heavy spring storms only, so unchanged flows during light summer rains say nothing against it.

D.why: Birds are an incidental benefit of the wetlands. The conclusion is about river flows, and this choice doesn't touch it.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Ilves's conclusion?
stimulus: In 2024, twelve software firms in Tallinn moved their staff from a five-day to a four-day workweek with no change in pay. Over the following year, the share of employees who resigned fell at those firms. Economist Marta Ilves concluded that the shorter workweek caused the drop in resignations.
choices: Resignations fell at the trial firms but stayed level at similar firms that kept a five-day week.
Resignations fell by the same amount at similar firms that kept a five-day week that year.
Workers at the trial firms reported spending more time with their families during the year.
The trial firms kept a five-day week, while similar firms in the city moved to four days.
explanation: Ilves says the shorter week caused resignations to fall. That only holds if the drop happened because of the four-day week. If similar firms that kept five days saw the same drop, something other than the shorter week explains the fall in resignations.

A.why: You answered the opposite question. A drop only at the four-day firms points to the shorter week as the cause, so this choice strengthens Ilves's conclusion.

C.why: Time with family is a side effect of the shorter week. It says nothing about whether the four-day week caused fewer resignations.

D.why: This flips the setup. The passage says the trial firms moved to a four-day week, so this choice describes a study that didn't happen.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Penrose's claim?
stimulus: Surviving cloth from the Ashby dye works, which operated in northern England from 1782 to 1810, is a deep red. The works' account books record regular payments to Dutch merchants. On that basis, historian Clara Penrose claims that the red came from madder, a plant root that the Netherlands exported in large amounts.
choices: The Ashby account books show that the Dutch merchants were paid for shipments of madder.
Chemical tests show that the red in the Ashby cloth comes from an insect dye, not madder.
The same Dutch merchants also sold raw wool to several other English dye works of the era.
The surviving Ashby cloth is mostly blue, with only a few threads of red in its pattern.
explanation: Penrose claims that the red dye in the cloth was madder. Her claim depends on the cloth actually containing madder, not just on the works having bought something from Dutch merchants. A test showing the red comes from a different dye directly contradicts her claim.

A.why: You answered the opposite question. Proof that the payments were for madder backs Penrose up, so this choice strengthens her claim.

C.why: What the merchants sold to other works is beside the point. It doesn't tell you which dye made the Ashby cloth red.

D.why: The passage says the surviving cloth is a deep red. This choice describes cloth the text rules out.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Takeda's claim?
stimulus: Twenty copies survive of an 1830s woodblock print showing Mount Hiei. The copies vary in ink color, but each shows the same scene. In a woodblock print, the lines come from ridges carved into the block, so every copy pulled from one block shares the same carved lines. Art historian Jun Takeda claims that all twenty copies were printed from a single block.
choices: The carved outline of the mountain is identical in shape across all twenty copies.
The carved outline of the mountain differs in shape between some copies and others.
Some copies of the print were made in blue ink, while others were made in gray ink.
Every print the artist made in the 1830s was pulled from a single carved block.
explanation: For Takeda's claim to hold, every copy must share the same carved lines, because one block can produce only one set. If the mountain's carved outline changes shape from copy to copy, the copies can't all have come from one block.

A.why: You answered the opposite question. Identical carved lines are what a single block would produce, so this choice supports Takeda.

C.why: The passage already tells you that ink color varies. Color comes from the ink, not the carving, so it tells you nothing about how many blocks were used.

D.why: This choice backs Takeda and then stretches the claim to every print the artist made. You were asked to weaken the claim about these twenty copies.
